The largest release in a while. It started as a VPN container updating mid-download
and ended with the pipeline no longer depending on BitTorrent at all for most new
releases.

## Direct HTTPS downloads via Pixeldrain

One Pace publishes most recent releases three ways — magnet, `.torrent`, and a
Pixeldrain direct link — and only the first two were ever used. The direct link
is now preferred when offered.

This matters because it fails for **entirely different reasons** than BitTorrent.
A dead VPN port-forward leaves torrents at `stalledDL` with no peers; an HTTPS GET
doesn't care. The two transports now cover each other instead of sharing a single
point of failure. Measured throughput was 37–62 MB/s.

- Every transfer is gated on Pixeldrain's **live rate-limit API** rather than an
  assumption. One Pace's own paid bandwidth currently covers downloads of their
  files, so the 6 GB free allowance isn't consumed — but that is their
  subscription, not a guarantee, so the pipeline checks and defers to the torrent
  if it ever changes.
- Transfers **resume**: bytes land in `<name>.part` and are renamed on completion,
  so a restart mid-download continues via HTTP Range instead of starting over.
- Falls back to the torrent when the release has no direct link, the limits say
  no, or three transfer attempts fail.
- Coverage is ~97% of *recent* releases (~42% of the whole feed — the back
  catalogue mostly predates it and is already on disk).

Set `DOWNLOAD_SOURCE=torrent` to keep the previous behaviour.

## One release per episode, decided before downloading

A feed batch lists a re-release alongside the release it supersedes, and the two
took different code paths — the new hash isn't catalogued yet so it went
provisional, the old one resolved cleanly. Neither branch knew about the other,
so **both were queued and both were downloaded**, and the import guard then
discarded the loser. The right library, bought at full price: ~780 MB wasted in
one observed batch.

Placement now happens for every feed item before anything is queued, and one
release per episode survives — the one the catalog can't place, which by the same
rule the coverage report uses is the newer of the two. The decision no longer
depends on feed order.

Two cheaper checks joined it, both of which previously ran only *after* a
gigabyte had moved: a release already in the library, and one that would be a
downgrade, are now skipped before the download starts.

## Resilience

The pipeline now assumes its dependencies are unreliable, because they are:

- **Stalled downloads are visible.** A new `Downloads` health check warns on
  anything that hasn't advanced in 3 hours. Six torrents previously sat stalled
  for seven hours with nothing anywhere reporting it.
- **A torrent removed from qBittorrent no longer strands its episode.** Completion
  was checked by asking whether the torrent had finished; one that had vanished
  simply answered "not yet", every 30 seconds, forever.
- **Failures retry themselves** — up to 3 attempts at 5m/20m/60m, so an
  environmental fault recovers without anyone pressing **Retry failed**.
- **Connection blips are retried** at the request level, dropping the session
  cookie first in case the client restarted.

## Also fixed

**"Downloaded file not found" when the torrent carried a different CRC32.** A feed
entry can advertise a hash the torrent doesn't contain — One Pace re-uploads an
episode and the entry still names the superseded release. The download succeeded
but the CRC-keyed lookup found nothing, and the episode failed with the file
sitting right there. The importer now falls back to the torrent's actual contents.

## Upgrading

Pull and restart. The `download_via`, `pixeldrain_id`, progress and retry columns
are added automatically on first boot. Nothing to click: anything stranded in
`pending` is picked up by the startup cycle.

If you would rather not have the app make direct HTTPS requests — for example
because your torrent traffic goes through a VPN and you want everything to — set
`DOWNLOAD_SOURCE=torrent` before starting.
